The interactive simulation below lets you experience this process firsthand.

A steep downhill slope means “move this way, fast!” A flat area means “we might be close.”
**Updates the position**, it takes a step in the direction that reduces the loss, scaled by the **learning rate**.

statements.quote: Plain momentum is a heavy ball rolling downhill: it builds up speed from past gradients, which is great, until it overshoots a valley.
The ball doesn't know to slow down before the slope reverses.
Nesterov's fix is small but clever: instead of measuring the slope *where you are*, measure it *where you're about to be*.
You take the momentum step first (a guess about your future position), then correct based on the gradient there:
Compare this with plain momentum — the only difference is that the gradient is now evaluated at $\theta - \beta v_{t-1}$ instead of at $\theta$.
It's a one-line change, but the ball is now noticeably more responsive: it slows down when it sees the slope curving up ahead, instead of running off the cliff and catching itself on the rebound.
\cite[Nesterov (1983)]{nesterov1983method} introduced the accelerated method; his 2004 book is the standard exposition (\cite[Nesterov, 2004]{nesterov2004introductory}).
In practice NAG typically shaves a few percent off training time on RNNs and other models with strong gradient curvature (\cite[Ruder, 2016]{ruder2016overview}).
SGD uses one global learning rate for every parameter.
But the world isn't uniform.
In a language model, the embedding for "the" gets a gradient signal on almost every batch; the embedding for "quokka" gets one gradient per million tokens.
Treating them the same is wasteful: "the" gets over-updated and "quokka" gets starved.
Parameters that have received large or frequent gradients get *smaller* effective steps (the denominator is large); parameters that have received small or rare gradients get *larger* effective steps.
The $\epsilon$ (usually $10^{-8}$) is just a guard against dividing by zero on the very first step.
Think of it as a per-parameter GPS that slows down for crowded streets and speeds up on empty roads.
Adagrad's own motivating setting was large-scale learning with sparse features, where rare but predictive coordinates — the paper's “needles in haystacks” — need larger steps \cite{duchi2011adagrad}.
RMSprop and Adadelta were developed independently around the same time and share the same core idea — a decaying average of squared gradients instead of Adagrad's ever-growing sum.
statements.section: Adadelta and RMSprop — Stop the Shrink

statements.quote: RMSprop is Adadelta's first ingredient with a fixed global learning rate ($\gamma = 0.9$, $\eta = 0.001$ in Hinton's slides); Adadelta adds the second ingredient, the RMS of past updates, and so needs no learning rate at all.
statements.section: Adadelta and RMSprop — Stop the Shrink

statements.quote: Zeiler's motivation was that the *units* of the RMSprop update don't match the units of $\theta$; replacing $\eta$ with the RMS of past parameter updates, $\mathrm{RMS}[\Delta\theta]_{t-1}$, fixes the dimensional mismatch.
statements.section: Adadelta and RMSprop — Stop the Shrink

statements.quote: Nadam is what you get when you apply the Nesterov trick to Adam.
The fix from \citeauthor{dozat2016nadam} (\citeyear{dozat2016nadam}) is one line: replace the previous momentum vector $\hat{m}_{t-1}$ in the Adam update with the *current* one $\hat{m}_t$:
It's a one-line modification, but it makes Adam's momentum term "look ahead" the same way Nesterov does, which tends to give modestly faster convergence on tasks with strong gradient curvature.
Adam isn't always the best.

Practitioners noticed that Adam can fail to converge on some problems, and \citeauthor{reddi2018amsgrad} (\citeyear{reddi2018amsgrad}) pinned down a cause: the EMA of squared gradients can *forget* large but rare gradients, so the effective step can grow again.
Their counterexample is a simple convex online problem, not a full network.
This guarantees a non-increasing effective step size, which restores the convergence guarantees that Adam lacks.
In practice AMSGrad sometimes matches Adam, sometimes loses to it; the empirical comparison was messier than the theory suggested, and most practitioners stuck with Adam.
\citetitle{loshchilov2019adamw} (\citealternativetitle{loshchilov2019adamw}) decouples them.

statements.quote: The cleanest family tree above doesn't mean Adam (or AdamW) is always the right choice.

\citeauthor{ruder2016overview}'s survey (\citeyear{ruder2016overview}) already noted the wrinkle: for convolutional networks on ImageNet, SGD with momentum and a careful learning-rate schedule often matches or beats Adam.

The intuition is sharp — SGD's noisier updates act as an implicit regularizer (they keep the ball bouncing, which helps it escape sharp minima), and a cosine or step-decay schedule gives the optimizer more chances to settle into a flat basin over time.
The pragmatic rule of thumb: **start with AdamW**.
If you have the compute for a careful learning-rate sweep and you need every last fraction of a percent of accuracy, try SGD-with-momentum with a cosine schedule.

For transformers and large language models specifically, AdamW dominates, because the per-parameter adaptivity genuinely matters when individual weights (especially in token embeddings) see wildly different gradient magnitudes.
Don't reach for anything else unless you have a specific reason to.
The learning rate is rarely held constant in practice.

Step decay lowered it at fixed epochs in early image models \cite{ruder2016overview}; \cite[Goyal et al. (2017)]{goyal2017largebatch} coupled a linear warm-up to the linear scaling rule for large batches; \cite[Loshchilov & Hutter (2016)]{loshchilov2016sgdr} replaced the step with a cosine that anneals to zero and restarts.
The schedule is itself a hyperparameter: its shape interacts with batch size and optimizer, which is why a search that tunes only the initial rate can miss most of the gain.
The effect is that every update direction is scaled to comparable size, so no single singular direction dominates a step.

In practice Muon is used only for the hidden 2-D weight matrices inside the network; embeddings, the output head, and 1-D parameters such as norms and biases stay on AdamW, because orthogonalization is not meaningful there (\cite[Jordan, 2024]{jordan2024muon}).
At trillion-parameter scale the attention logits can explode when the query and key weights grow together.

**MuonClip**, used to train Kimi K2, adds a QK-clip that rescales those weights when their logits exceed a threshold, making the optimizer stable enough for a 1T-parameter mixture-of-experts run (\cite[Kimi Team, 2025]{kimi2025k2}).
Muon is still young, but it is the first concrete evidence that the AdamW monoculture may not be permanent.
In \citeyear{sgd}, **Herbert Robbins** and **Sutton Monro** published their paper “\citetitle{sgd}”, introducing the **Robbins-Monro Process**.
This was the first formalization of **Stochastic Approximation**, which allows finding roots or optima using noisy samples.
Robbins and Monro found a root of a noisy function.

A year later, \cite[Kiefer & Wolfowitz (1952)]{kiefer1952stochastic} turned the idea into a search for a maximum: observe the regression function at two nearby points, form a finite-difference estimate of the slope, and step along it with a shrinking step size.

This is stochastic gradient ascent in all but name, and it made the noisy-optimization framework usable when the gradient itself cannot be observed, the situation that motivates derivative-free optimization.
Stochastic approximation is the ancestor of SGD: the same root-finding recursion becomes the SGD update when the function is the loss gradient and the root is its zero.
Their iterative formula reads
Cauchy's method was not yet our gradient descent: he minimized a sum of squared residuals to solve equations, not a training loss.
The idea surfaced again independently in 1907–1908, when \cite[Hadamard (1908)]{hadamard1908} used steepest descent in a memoir on clamped elastic plates.

Only with the rise of numerical optimization in the mid-twentieth century did the same step rule become a general-purpose minimizer, and only with backpropagation did it become the engine of a neural network.
While Cauchy provided the “map” for downhill movement, the challenge for AI was applying this to complex, multi-layered networks.

statements.quote: To understand *why* Adam has become the industry standard, consider its key difference from SGD.
SGD applies a single, global learning rate to every parameter in the model, whether that parameter is updated thousands of times per batch or only once in a blue moon.

Adam, short for **Adaptive Moment Estimation**, maintains a *per-parameter* running estimate of both the **first moment** (the mean of gradients) and the **second moment** (the mean of squared gradients).

This means parameters that receive sparse, infrequent gradient signals, like the embeddings for rare words, automatically get larger effective learning rates, because their second moment estimate stays small.
Conversely, parameters that are updated densely and frequently get smaller effective steps, preventing them from overshooting.
In essence, Adam doesn't just navigate the loss landscape, it *reshapes* the landscape to appear more uniform for each parameter independently.
This is especially critical in NLP, where token frequencies follow a **\cite[Zipf distribution]{zipf1949human}**: a few words like “the” appear constantly, while most words are rare.
Without Adam, rare tokens would be starved of meaningful updates, and common tokens would dominate the optimization.
Adam's per-parameter adaptivity elegantly solves this imbalance, which is a major reason it is the default optimizer for training modern large language models.
The lineage that leads here is the cleanest story in the optimizer zoo.

Adagrad introduced per-parameter learning rates; Adadelta and RMSprop fixed Adagrad's flaw that the accumulated denominator shrank the effective step toward zero; Adam added a bias-corrected first moment (essentially momentum with a different normalization) on top.
\citeauthor{ruder2016overview} (\citeyear{ruder2016overview}) walks through each derivation, and that genealogy is the one this lesson has been climbing toward.
| Problem | Symptom | Solution |
| **Learning rate too high** | Loss oscillates wildly or explodes to infinity | Reduce LR by a factor of 10; use a learning rate scheduler |
| **Learning rate too low** | Loss decreases painfully slowly; training takes forever | Increase LR; consider warmup schedules |
| **Stuck in local minimum** | Loss plateaus at a suboptimal value | Try Momentum or Adam; increase LR temporarily; restart from a different position |
| **Overfitting** | Training loss is low but validation loss rises | Add regularization (dropout, weight decay); reduce model size; get more data |
You may have seen the advice that the *best* learning rate is the largest one that "just barely" doesn't diverge.

statements.quote: That is not folklore; it names a sharp, studied regime called the **edge of stability**.
statements.section: The Edge of Stability: why the best learning rate sits on a knife-edge

statements.quote: When the learning rate $\eta$ is large enough that a single step would overshoot a sharp region, gradient descent does **not** blow up.
statements.section: The Edge of Stability: why the best learning rate sits on a knife-edge

statements.quote: Instead it **locks** onto that sharp region and *oscillates* at its rim, with the largest curvature (the sharpness, the top Hessian eigenvalue) settling right around $\lambda_{\max} \approx 2/\eta$ while the loss still drifts downward (\cite[Cohen et al., 2021]{cohen2021edgeofstability}; \cite[Arora et al., 2022]{arora2022edgeofstability}).

statements.quote: The optimizer is balancing on the knife-edge of a sharp minimum, and — surprisingly — it *prefers* those edges over the flat bottoms it would otherwise settle into.

statements.quote: A high $\eta$ that makes the loss *oscillate but keep falling* is not a bug to fix — it is the network running at the edge of stability, a regime many modern training curves actually live in.

statements.quote: The practical read: if your loss oscillates but trends steadily down, you are on the edge, and you can often stay there or push a little further rather than immediately dialing the learning rate back.

blocks.quote: The Rest of the Optimizer Family
blocks.section: The Rest of the Optimizer Family

blocks.quote: SGD, Momentum, and Adam are the headliners, but the zoo is bigger. Each of the optimizers below was invented to fix a specific failure of the previous one. Reading them in order is reading the most productive argument in modern optimization.
blocks.section: The Rest of the Optimizer Family

blocks.quote: Nesterov Accelerated Gradient (NAG)
Plain momentum is a heavy ball rolling downhill: it builds up speed from past gradients, which is great, until it overshoots a valley. The ball doesn't know to slow down before the slope reverses.

Nesterov's fix is small but clever: instead of measuring the slope *where you are*, measure it *where you're about to be*. You take the momentum step first (a guess about your future position), then correct based on the gradient there:

Compare this with plain momentum — the only difference is that the gradient is now evaluated at $\theta - \beta v_{t-1}$ instead of at $\theta$. It's a one-line change, but the ball is now noticeably more responsive: it slows down when it sees the slope curving up ahead, instead of running off the cliff and catching itself on the rebound. \cite[Nesterov (1983)]{nesterov1983method} introduced the accelerated method; his 2004 book is the standard exposition (\cite[Nesterov, 2004]{nesterov2004introductory}). In practice NAG typically shaves a few percent off training time on RNNs and other models with strong gradient curvature (\cite[Ruder, 2016]{ruder2016overview}).
Adagrad — The Per-Parameter GPS

SGD uses one global learning rate for every parameter. But the world isn't uniform. In a language model, the embedding for "the" gets a gradient signal on almost every batch; the embedding for "quokka" gets one gradient per million tokens. Treating them the same is wasteful: "the" gets over-updated and "quokka" gets starved.

Parameters that have received large or frequent gradients get *smaller* effective steps (the denominator is large); parameters that have received small or rare gradients get *larger* effective steps. The $\epsilon$ (usually $10^{-8}$) is just a guard against dividing by zero on the very first step. Think of it as a per-parameter GPS that slows down for crowded streets and speeds up on empty roads. Adagrad's own motivating setting was large-scale learning with sparse features, where rare but predictive coordinates — the paper's “needles in haystacks” — need larger steps \cite{duchi2011adagrad}.
Adadelta and RMSprop — Stop the Shrink
blocks.section: Adadelta and RMSprop — Stop the Shrink

blocks.quote: RMSprop and Adadelta were developed independently around the same time and share the same core idea — a decaying average of squared gradients instead of Adagrad's ever-growing sum. RMSprop is Adadelta's first ingredient with a fixed global learning rate ($\gamma = 0.9$, $\eta = 0.001$ in Hinton's slides); Adadelta adds the second ingredient, the RMS of past updates, and so needs no learning rate at all. Zeiler's motivation was that the *units* of the RMSprop update don't match the units of $\theta$; replacing $\eta$ with the RMS of past parameter updates, $\mathrm{RMS}[\Delta\theta]_{t-1}$, fixes the dimensional mismatch.
blocks.section: Adadelta and RMSprop — Stop the Shrink

blocks.quote: AdaMax — A More Stable Denominator
Nadam — Adam, but Look Ahead

Nadam is what you get when you apply the Nesterov trick to Adam. The fix from \citeauthor{dozat2016nadam} (\citeyear{dozat2016nadam}) is one line: replace the previous momentum vector $\hat{m}_{t-1}$ in the Adam update with the *current* one $\hat{m}_t$:
It's a one-line modification, but it makes Adam's momentum term "look ahead" the same way Nesterov does, which tends to give modestly faster convergence on tasks with strong gradient curvature.
AMSGrad — Fixing a Convergence Flaw

Adam isn't always the best. Practitioners noticed that Adam can fail to converge on some problems, and \citeauthor{reddi2018amsgrad} (\citeyear{reddi2018amsgrad}) pinned down a cause: the EMA of squared gradients can *forget* large but rare gradients, so the effective step can grow again. Their counterexample is a simple convex online problem, not a full network.

This guarantees a non-increasing effective step size, which restores the convergence guarantees that Adam lacks. In practice AMSGrad sometimes matches Adam, sometimes loses to it; the empirical comparison was messier than the theory suggested, and most practitioners stuck with Adam.
AdamW — Fixing the Weight Decay Bug
blocks.section: AdamW — Fixing the Weight Decay Bug

blocks.quote: \citetitle{loshchilov2019adamw} (\citealternativetitle{loshchilov2019adamw}) decouples them. Weight decay is applied *directly* to the weights, not through the gradient:
blocks.section: AdamW — Fixing the Weight Decay Bug

blocks.quote: It's a one-line change, but it makes weight decay behave the way every other optimizer's weight decay does, and it decouples weight decay from the adaptive gradient update. **AdamW is now the default optimizer for training transformers** in practice — Llama and Stable Diffusion use it, while the original BERT and GPT-3 recipes still used Adam; BERT's recipe applied weight decay through the loss.
blocks.section: AdamW — Fixing the Weight Decay Bug

blocks.quote: Adam was posted in December 2014 and published at ICLR 2015 \cite{adam}; AdamW followed as a 2017 preprint and an ICLR 2019 paper \cite{loshchilov2019adamw}. The gap matters: for three years the default recipe was “Adam with L2”, and the decoupled version spread as transformers made weight decay a first-class knob. The pair is a good example of how optimizer history actually runs — a fix can be mathematically small, sit in public for two years, and still change practice only when the surrounding models make its advantage visible.
blocks.section: AdamW — Fixing the Weight Decay Bug

blocks.quote: When Adam Doesn't Win

The cleanest family tree above doesn't mean Adam (or AdamW) is always the right choice. \citeauthor{ruder2016overview}'s survey (\citeyear{ruder2016overview}) already noted the wrinkle: for convolutional networks on ImageNet, SGD with momentum and a careful learning-rate schedule often matches or beats Adam. The intuition is sharp — SGD's noisier updates act as an implicit regularizer (they keep the ball bouncing, which helps it escape sharp minima), and a cosine or step-decay schedule gives the optimizer more chances to settle into a flat basin over time.

The pragmatic rule of thumb: **start with AdamW**. If you have the compute for a careful learning-rate sweep and you need every last fraction of a percent of accuracy, try SGD-with-momentum with a cosine schedule. For transformers and large language models specifically, AdamW dominates, because the per-parameter adaptivity genuinely matters when individual weights (especially in token embeddings) see wildly different gradient magnitudes. Don't reach for anything else unless you have a specific reason to.
Learning-Rate Schedules

The learning rate is rarely held constant in practice. Step decay lowered it at fixed epochs in early image models \cite{ruder2016overview}; \cite[Goyal et al. (2017)]{goyal2017largebatch} coupled a linear warm-up to the linear scaling rule for large batches; \cite[Loshchilov & Hutter (2016)]{loshchilov2016sgdr} replaced the step with a cosine that anneals to zero and restarts. The schedule is itself a hyperparameter: its shape interacts with batch size and optimizer, which is why a search that tunes only the initial rate can miss most of the gain.
Muon — orthogonalize the update

The effect is that every update direction is scaled to comparable size, so no single singular direction dominates a step. In practice Muon is used only for the hidden 2-D weight matrices inside the network; embeddings, the output head, and 1-D parameters such as norms and biases stay on AdamW, because orthogonalization is not meaningful there (\cite[Jordan, 2024]{jordan2024muon}).

At trillion-parameter scale the attention logits can explode when the query and key weights grow together. **MuonClip**, used to train Kimi K2, adds a QK-clip that rescales those weights when their logits exceed a threshold, making the optimizer stable enough for a 1T-parameter mixture-of-experts run (\cite[Kimi Team, 2025]{kimi2025k2}). Muon is still young, but it is the first concrete evidence that the AdamW monoculture may not be permanent.
History of Optimizers

In \citeyear{sgd}, **Herbert Robbins** and **Sutton Monro** published their paper “\citetitle{sgd}”, introducing the **Robbins-Monro Process**. This was the first formalization of **Stochastic Approximation**, which allows finding roots or optima using noisy samples.

Robbins and Monro found a root of a noisy function. A year later, \cite[Kiefer & Wolfowitz (1952)]{kiefer1952stochastic} turned the idea into a search for a maximum: observe the regression function at two nearby points, form a finite-difference estimate of the slope, and step along it with a shrinking step size. This is stochastic gradient ascent in all but name, and it made the noisy-optimization framework usable when the gradient itself cannot be observed, the situation that motivates derivative-free optimization.
Stochastic approximation is the ancestor of SGD: the same root-finding recursion becomes the SGD update when the function is the loss gradient and the root is its zero. Their iterative formula reads

Cauchy's method was not yet our gradient descent: he minimized a sum of squared residuals to solve equations, not a training loss. The idea surfaced again independently in 1907–1908, when \cite[Hadamard (1908)]{hadamard1908} used steepest descent in a memoir on clamped elastic plates. Only with the rise of numerical optimization in the mid-twentieth century did the same step rule become a general-purpose minimizer, and only with backpropagation did it become the engine of a neural network.
The Bridge to Modern AI: Backpropagation
blocks.section: The Bridge to Modern AI: Backpropagation

blocks.quote: While Cauchy provided the “map” for downhill movement, the challenge for AI was applying this to complex, multi-layered networks. This required a way to distribute the blame for an error across millions of internal “neurons.”
blocks.section: The Bridge to Modern AI: Backpropagation

blocks.quote: Why Adam Dominates

To understand *why* Adam has become the industry standard, consider its key difference from SGD. SGD applies a single, global learning rate to every parameter in the model, whether that parameter is updated thousands of times per batch or only once in a blue moon. Adam, short for **Adaptive Moment Estimation**, maintains a *per-parameter* running estimate of both the **first moment** (the mean of gradients) and the **second moment** (the mean of squared gradients).

This means parameters that receive sparse, infrequent gradient signals, like the embeddings for rare words, automatically get larger effective learning rates, because their second moment estimate stays small. Conversely, parameters that are updated densely and frequently get smaller effective steps, preventing them from overshooting. In essence, Adam doesn't just navigate the loss landscape, it *reshapes* the landscape to appear more uniform for each parameter independently.

This is especially critical in NLP, where token frequencies follow a **\cite[Zipf distribution]{zipf1949human}**: a few words like “the” appear constantly, while most words are rare. Without Adam, rare tokens would be starved of meaningful updates, and common tokens would dominate the optimization. Adam's per-parameter adaptivity elegantly solves this imbalance, which is a major reason it is the default optimizer for training modern large language models.

The lineage that leads here is the cleanest story in the optimizer zoo. Adagrad introduced per-parameter learning rates; Adadelta and RMSprop fixed Adagrad's flaw that the accumulated denominator shrank the effective step toward zero; Adam added a bias-corrected first moment (essentially momentum with a different normalization) on top. \citeauthor{ruder2016overview} (\citeyear{ruder2016overview}) walks through each derivation, and that genealogy is the one this lesson has been climbing toward.
Common Pitfalls & Practical Tips
| Problem | Symptom | Solution |
| **Learning rate too high** | Loss oscillates wildly or explodes to infinity | Reduce LR by a factor of 10; use a learning rate scheduler |
| **Learning rate too low** | Loss decreases painfully slowly; training takes forever | Increase LR; consider warmup schedules |
| **Stuck in local minimum** | Loss plateaus at a suboptimal value | Try Momentum or Adam; increase LR temporarily; restart from a different position |
| **Overfitting** | Training loss is low but validation loss rises | Add regularization (dropout, weight decay); reduce model size; get more data |
The Edge of Stability: why the best learning rate sits on a knife-edge
blocks.section: The Edge of Stability: why the best learning rate sits on a knife-edge

blocks.quote: You may have seen the advice that the *best* learning rate is the largest one that "just barely" doesn't diverge. That is not folklore; it names a sharp, studied regime called the **edge of stability**. When the learning rate $\eta$ is large enough that a single step would overshoot a sharp region, gradient descent does **not** blow up. Instead it **locks** onto that sharp region and *oscillates* at its rim, with the largest curvature (the sharpness, the top Hessian eigenvalue) settling right around $\lambda_{\max} \approx 2/\eta$ while the loss still drifts downward (\cite[Cohen et al., 2021]{cohen2021edgeofstability}; \cite[Arora et al., 2022]{arora2022edgeofstability}). The optimizer is balancing on the knife-edge of a sharp minimum, and — surprisingly — it *prefers* those edges over the flat bottoms it would otherwise settle into.
blocks.section: The Edge of Stability: why the best learning rate sits on a knife-edge

blocks.quote: This reframes the "learning rate too high" row in the table above. A high $\eta$ that makes the loss *oscillate but keep falling* is not a bug to fix — it is the network running at the edge of stability, a regime many modern training curves actually live in. The practical read: if your loss oscillates but trends steadily down, you are on the edge, and you can often stay there or push a little further rather than immediately dialing the learning rate back.
blocks.section: The Edge of Stability: why the best learning rate sits on a knife-edge
